title: Wireshark: Capturing and Analysing Web Traffic
description: Students capture live network traffic using Wireshark, then isolate and analyse DNS queries, TCP handshakes, TLS negotiation, and HTTP payloads to understand what travels across the wire.
objective: Students will use Wireshark to capture packets, apply protocol filters, and annotate at least four distinct protocol interactions — demonstrating practical understanding of how DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP operate at the packet level.

steps.title: Install Wireshark and Start a Capture
steps.instructions:
Download and install Wireshark from https://www.wireshark.org/download.html

Launch Wireshark. On the start screen, you will see a list of network interfaces with activity graphs. Select your **active interface** (the one showing traffic — typically `Ethernet 0` or `Wi-Fi`).

Click the **blue shark-fin** icon (or press `Ctrl+E`) to begin capturing. Leave it running.

> **Important:** Wireshark may require elevated privileges on Linux. Run:
> ```
> sudo wireshark
> # OR add yourself to the wireshark group:
> sudo usermod -aG wireshark $USER
> ```

You should immediately see packets appearing. This confirms the capture is working.

steps.title: Generate Traffic: DNS, HTTP, and HTTPS
steps.instructions:
With the capture running, open a terminal and run the following commands to generate specific traffic types:

**Generate DNS traffic:**
```bash
nslookup wikipedia.org
nslookup github.com 8.8.8.8
```

**Generate HTTP (unencrypted) traffic:**
Open a browser and navigate to:
```
http://neverssl.com
```
This site intentionally serves unencrypted HTTP — ideal for Wireshark inspection.

**Generate HTTPS (TLS) traffic:**
```
https://example.com
https://wikipedia.org
```

**Generate ICMP traffic (ping):**
```bash
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
```

Wait 30 seconds, then stop the capture by pressing `Ctrl+E` or clicking the red stop square.

steps.title: Filter and Analyse DNS Traffic
steps.instructions:
In Wireshark's filter bar (green bar at the top), type `dns` and press Enter.

You should see DNS query and response pairs. Click on a DNS **query** packet (the one going *to* port 53).

In the packet details panel, expand **Domain Name System (query)** and find:
- The queried name (e.g., `wikipedia.org`)
- The query type (should be `A` for IPv4)

Now click the corresponding DNS **response** (same transaction ID, direction reversed). Find:
- The answer section — note the returned IP address
- The TTL value (how long to cache the result)

**Screenshot:** Take a screenshot showing the DNS query and response. Draw arrows or annotate (in any image editor) pointing to: transaction ID, query name, record type, returned IP, TTL.

**Tip:** `Right-click → Follow → UDP Stream` shows the full DNS conversation as decoded text.

steps.title: Identify a TCP Three-Way Handshake
steps.instructions:
Clear the filter and type: `tcp.flags.syn == 1`

This shows all TCP SYN packets — the start of new connections. Click on any SYN packet.

In the details panel, note:
- Source IP and destination IP
- Source port (ephemeral, e.g., 52341) and destination port (e.g., 80 or 443)
- Flags: `SYN` is set, `ACK` is not

Now modify the filter to: `tcp and (ip.addr == [the destination IP from above])`

You should see the full 3-way handshake sequence:
1. **SYN** — client to server (Flags: SYN)
2. **SYN-ACK** — server to client (Flags: SYN, ACK)
3. **ACK** — client to server (Flags: ACK)

**Screenshot:** Capture the 3-packet handshake. Annotate each packet with its role (SYN / SYN-ACK / ACK) and the port numbers shown.

```bash
# Verify: what does the source port number tell you?
# Ephemeral ports (1024-65535) are assigned by the OS to outbound connections.
# Well-known destination ports (80, 443) identify the service.
```

steps.title: Inspect TLS Handshake and Compare with HTTP
steps.instructions:
**Part A — TLS Client Hello:**
Apply the filter: `tls.handshake.type == 1`

This shows only TLS Client Hello packets. Click one and expand **Transport Layer Security → TLSv1.3 Record Layer → Handshake Protocol: Client Hello**.

Document:
- TLS version supported
- At least 3 cipher suites offered (e.g., `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`)
- SNI (Server Name Indication) — the target hostname in plaintext

**Screenshot:** Show the expanded Client Hello with cipher suites visible.

**Part B — HTTP payload visibility:**
Apply filter: `http`

Click any HTTP packet and expand **Hypertext Transfer Protocol**. If you visited `http://neverssl.com`, you should see the full GET request including:
- The exact URL path requested
- User-Agent (browser version)
- Any cookies sent

Compare: With `tls` filter, the same level of detail is not visible — you only see encrypted records.

**Written submission:** In 3–5 sentences, explain what an attacker on the same Wi-Fi network could learn from the HTTP traffic versus the HTTPS traffic. Include what SNI leaks even in TLS connections.

expected_output: Students submit: (1) A PDF or document containing 4 annotated screenshots — DNS, TCP handshake, TLS Client Hello, HTTP payload. (2) Written answers to the comparison question. (3) A list of at least 3 cipher suites from the Client Hello. Each screenshot must have labels or arrows identifying the key fields described in each step.
